Customs tariff-35. Hops, per pound: British preferential tariff, 6 cents; intermediate tariff, 10 cents; general tariff, 16 cents.

When the committee rose last night I was discussing this item. I am interested in it from the standpoint of employment because it means a considerable amount of employment to those working in the industry in the district I have the honour to represent, and it is also of importance to neighbouring cities. In the harvesting season we employ in the industry about 3,000 people and hundreds are employed the year round. There is no branch of agriculture in which as much employment is afforded per acre as hop growing. I appreciate the remarks the minister made last evening with regard to encouraging this industry, and I hope he will do his best to see that Canadian hops are purchased by the consumers of this country.
There is just one other point I should like to raise. I notice that a little further on a grant is made by way of reduction of tariff to the brewers of the Irish Free State. It occurs to me that some years ago an agreement was entered into between Ireland and, I think, New Zealand, whereby there was a removal or reduction of the tariff on products of the brewing industry entering New Zealand, and on the other hand New Zealand hops were admitted into Ireland on more favourable terms. When the time comes to consider the empire agreements, perhaps Canada may be enabled to sell to the brewers of Ireland a certain quantity of our hops. I hope the minister will bear this in mind.

I have no objection, as a matter of policy, to that; I think it is in the interests of the agricultural producers of this country that there should be some protection. 'Mr. DUNNING:	There is a considerable
amendment both in wording and in rates. Perhaps I had better read my notes, in order that the committee may be fulled seized of the matter and so that there may be no misapprehension as to the effect.
Up to the present time unmanufactured tobacco enumerated under tariff item 142 has been free of duty upon all tariff. That is to say, it has been imported nominally free of customs duties, but immediately under the Excise Act became subject to excise duties of 40 cents per pound on unstemmed leaf and 60 cents per pound on stemmed leaf. To carry out an undertaking given to Southern Rhodesia under the conference agreements of 1932 it is now proposed first to establish a preference on both stemmed and unstemmed tobacco of the type commonly known as Turkish or Oriental, and second to transfer the duties from the excise to the customs realm. It will be remembered that when we were dealing with the excise amendments these excise taxes were cancelled. The proposal to transfer this item to the customs realm is of course inevitable if the undertaking to Rhodesia is to be carried out, since it would seem to be undesirable if not indeed impossible to provide preferential treatment in the excise field of taxation as distinct from the customs field.
It is proposed therefore, in brief, to divide the item in such a manner as to separate the so called Turkish type of tobacco from all other types and, in respect of the Turkish type, to reduce the British preferential rates of duty from 40 cents to 20 cents per pound on the unstemmed and from 60 cents to 30 cents on the stemmed. The requirements
of the Canadian tobacco industry and therefore of the Canadian tobacco consuming public demand the use of a certain amount of the Turkish type of tobacco. It is estimated that the Canadian use of tobaccos of the Turkish type amounts to about 300,000 pounds per annum, all of which up to the present has been supplied from non-empire countries, chiefly Macedonia, Greece and Abyssinia. I do not suppose we are getting much from there just now, but this has been one of the few articles we have imported from that country. In recent years Southern Rhodesia has established quite a reputation for Turkish type tobacco, and the Union of South Africa is known to be producing tobacco of this type which has gained commercial favour. The Rhodesian product is finding acceptance in the British market, and in establishing the preference now proposed the government feels that it may be giving Southern Rhodesia a greater opportunity to cater to Canadian requirements in this particular product. There is no reason to feel that the preference now being granted under the British .preference to Turkish type tobacco will react in any way whatsoever on the Canadian production of those types which Canada has demonstrated her ability to produce and sell. It is, however, confidently expected that empire sources of supply will fill the demand of this market and that by accepting tobacco from Southern Rhodesia Canada may make it possible for that country to provide a wider market than at present for certain Canadian commodities. I am assured that the change here proposed has no bearing whatsoever on the Canadian production of tobacco, which is of an entirely different type from that now being given a preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am reading the small print in the item in an effort to answer the hon. member's question. In the item I find these words:
... produced by any process other than hand painting or drawing, and having any advertisement or advertising matter printed, lithographed or stamped thereon, or attached thereto.
There is no change in the wording in that regard. The change is in the rates, with a provision of a minimum ad valorem duty of 271 per cent under the intermediate tariff. Prior to September, 1930, the rates were 10 cents, 15 cents and 15 cents per pound. Under the budget of September, 1930, there was added to the item a proviso that the minimum duty under the, general tariff should not be less than 35 per cent ad valorem. Following the imperial conference of 1932 the British preferential rate was reduced to 5 cents per pound. The result of the extension of the intermediate rate to the United States on January 1 of this year was that imports of printed matter, n.o.p., from that country dutiable under this item paid a specific duty of 121 cents per pound, but-were, not subject alternatively to any minimum ad valorem imposed.
An analysis of the imports from the United States under the item shows that, in the fiscal year 1935, had these imports been dutiable at the rate of fifteen cents per pound without any ad valorem, they would have paid $315,700 in duty. Actually however they paid duties of $373,800, on a declared value of $826,000. Thus the ad valorem incidence of the double rate on imports from the United States under the general tariff in 1935 was
	, [jj
something over forty-five per cent. If we assumed that the same volume and value of imports enter at the existing intermediate specific duty of 121 cents per pound, they would pay a duty to total $263,000, or 31-8 per cent ad valorem. In other words the ad valorem equivalent of the intermediate duty of 121 cents per pound would be, on the volume and value of last year's imports from the United States, somewhat less than thirty-two per cent. However, the fact must be remembered that a specific duty on a poundage basis has a varying and unequal effect when spread over a wide field of printed matter, such as is covered by this item. It might represent a relatively high rate ad valorem on certain printed matter, and a ridiculously low rate on other matter. Having regard to the unequal incidence of a specific duty on the very great volume of goods covered by this item, and also the wide disparity existing between the intermediate and general tariffs, we desire to impose under the intermediate tariff a safeguarding minimum ad valorem of 271 per cent, which I feel is not disproportionate to the minimum ad valorem of thirty-five per cent formerly effective under the general tariff on imports from the United States.
I should point out of course that the duty now proposed is not in any sense a double or compound duty, but is alternative in that the specific duty applies, except in those cases where it would have an ad valorem incidence of lower than 271 per cent, in which event the minimum ad valorem becomes effective.

It just amounted to this, that on the finest type of art work the degree of tariff worked out ad valorem to slightly under five per cent, whereas with respect to advertising in bulk of the cheaper type it might well run up to and did go as high as from thirty to forty per cent. By the means adopted here, of a specific duty but with a minimum ad valorem, it is hoped to equalize that factor.

I followed the hon.
gentleman; he need have no misapprehension in that regard. I only point out that we have reduced the duty payable on imports from the United States by 74 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: More than that.

It would be a little more having regard to value, but it still remains .124 cents a pound; there is no change in that It used to be 15 cents a pound under the intermediate, so there is 24 cents a pound less on advertising coming in from the United States, plus a reduction of 74 per cent ad valorem, if the conditions mentioned were to obtain; that is, a minimum of 274 per cent instead of 35 per cent. Now if our importations for the year ended March, 1935, from the United States, paying a minimum of 35 per cent and 15 cents a pound, were as large as the hon. gentleman indicated, not the whole $800,000 but a substantial part of it, I question whether ample protection has been given to the Canadian industry against the class of competition it has to meet. I recall pretty definitely that when we increased the rate it was in consequence of the advertising competition we had to meet; we made a minimum rate of 35 per cent as against the old rate, and that increase did have the effect of adding to employment in Canada and developing to no inconsiderable degree the artistic talents of Canadian workmen and workwomen in the various advertising agencies in the country.
The trade agreement, of course, necessitated our dealing with the intermediate tariff instead of the general. The United States had been on the general and are now on the intermediate, and dealing with the intermediate we have provided that they shall pay a rate of not less than 274 per cent ad valorem; but the base rate, instead of being 15 cents a pound, as it was for the year ended March 31, 1935, has become 124 cents a pound. So we have really done this: We

have reduced the base rate from 15 to 124 cents a pound on advertising coming in from the United States, which amounts to a considerable reduction, and then in addition we have said that in any event the duty paid on this advertising shall not be less than 274 per cent of its value, whereas for the year ended March 31, 1935, the ad valorem provision was 35 per cent. The two together must mean a very substantial additional competition to foe met by Canadians with a limited production as against the mass production of their great competitors.
Has the minister the figures of the United States imports as distinguished from other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The imports from the United States for the last few fiscal years expressed in dollars are as follows: 1931, $2,044,000. Three months of 1936 would be under the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I confess, Mr. Chairman, that I was more surprised at this item than at almost any other item with which I have had to deal in the tariff. The Canadian business in this one item amounts apparently to $15,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Enormous.

An enormous business. I could hardly credit it when it was first brought to my attention. I scarcely [DOT] thought it possible that we were producing so much, apart altogether from newspaper advertising. Our production amounted to $1,250,000 or $1,500,000 a month. I think it would have been well to leave that intermediate tariff at 35 per cent, having regard to what our own experience was. I have heard the reasons adduced against it, but I doubt, and there^ is some reason for it in the figures the minister has given, whether this will be sufficient protection. For three months of the period for which the minister gave the figures the duty was 124 cents a pound, without restriction, and it may well be that the steps now taken will tighten that up; I believe they will,

but whether or not it is ample for the maintenance of our $15,000,000 business, I cannot say. It did strike me, when I was looking at it, that it was questionable whether it was sufficient. I know that the minister is dealing with it from 'the point of view of what he thinks fair for the interests concerned, and if he thinks 27J cents is ample he must have good reason for so thinking. But having regard to my own experience and the magnitude of the item, of which I had no idea until it was first brought to my attention, I doubt whether we are warranted in substituting for the old 35 per cent rate a 27i per cent rate, added to the fact that we have made the poundage rate 2J cents less against United States imports. That is my fear; I hope I may be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have gone into the matter with some care, particularly having regard to the figures. As a matter of fact, there was a surprisingly small increase in the first three months relatively to what might have been expected.
It was $900,000 in the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Compared with $826,000 in the previous year. I find there are one or two things operating in connection with this item. There is no doubt that this does have an effect-
A very marked effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Having regard to the fact that there was $943,000 worth of imports out of a total business of $15,000,000, I felt, after examining all the factors, and not losing sight of the excise tax as-an additional consideration, that this was fair; and I must say I have had no representations to the contrary from any of the interests affected since it became known that this proposal was to be made. By and large, I think it will hit the mark.
I assume that the discrepancies in value for duty purposes on the poundage basis were not apparent prior to this change in the United States agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

While you had the poundage basis and the percentage rate, there was not the same difficulty as there has been since.

Mr. Ma-cNICOL:	Yes. I have in mind
a well known magazine, although I cannot at the moment recall the name of it. I was *told that in the case of that magazine the front page, which includes the back page, will come in free under this item, and that were it not for this item those particular pages would be printed in this country. But as on the other side they print a great number of the front pages to be sent out as window *displays, to attract public attention to the magazine, and all they have to do is to run off a few more copies, 1,500 or 2,000, and ship them into Canada to take care of the Canadian trade. That particular printer thought that this was a hardship to Canadian publishers, and it strikes me that way too. Again, if the original plates or electrotypes from which the articles in the last half of item 183 are printed were imported into this country, they would have to pay under item 473a, a 74 per cent duty. It does not seem reasonable that the finished article should come in free while the electrotype or plate that is imported for printing in Canada will have to pay a 74 per cent duty. The combination of those two items cannot do other than deprive Canadian workmen of employment. In fact I was told in the course of the conversation I mentioned that this item, in conjunction with the provisions of the Canada-United States trade agreement pertaining to the printing of American magazines, has resulted in the releasing in Toronto alone of 250 girls who were employed for binding, and in conjunction with this item an additional number of pressmen have been and will be laid off. I was in business for a long time, and I cannot see any other result of the adoption of this item than the reduction of employment in Canada. I know the minister does not want to do anything like that. I realize his sincerity and I am convinced that he, as much as anybody else, wants to provide work for Canadians. But here is a tariff provision which means reducing employment in Canada. I cannot see it in any other way. The American people themselves are convinced that it is going to work considerable benefit to them. I remember seeing a few days ago in one of the Toronto papers a dispatch from New York dated March 30 which had been republished in Toronto. One part of it reads as follows:
One striking result of the recently initiated reciprocal trade agreement with the United States has been a tremendous increase in sales of American magazines in the dominion, one magazine alone showing a gain of 125 per cent over last year. As a consequence the advertisement of American products in Canada has increased proportionately, and it is expected that this will result in a corresponding stimulus to American sales of all kinds.
If that be true-and I have no reason to doubt it-an increase of American sales in Canada as a result of these glorified catalogues which are now flooding our market cannot fail to reduce employment in Canada. I suggest to the minister that the item be divided in two. Let the first part of it end at the words, "published in Canada," and then make a new item covering "comic and pictorial sections, non-advertising, to be inserted in or folded with periodical publications entered for mailing purposes as second-class matter," and place whatever the minister considers to be a reasonable duty against the importation of these comic and pictorial sections, because if these latter are published in Canada it cannot result otherwise than in providing employment in printing, in the production of paper and ink and whatever else is required to produce them. In all sincerity I put that to the minister. I believe every member wishes to increase employment in this country, although all do not see the problem in the same way. I have tried to demonstrate, however imperfectly, that the item as it now appears cannot but result in reduction in employment in Canada, but if it were divided, the latter half taken out and a duty placed on the matter therein referred to, employment in Canada would benefit. I do not know whether the minister can do anything at the present time, but I hope that if he cannot he will do something about it later.

I can cover what I have to say before the minister replies. I regret that he has not seen fit to alter this item. Few items gave more concern to the late government than this one. It involves the question: are we doing the young children of Canada a service by putting on the free list the Katzenjammer kids and the Jiggses and that form of illustration that is coming into this country? Like most public men I am not unmindful of the effect of the influence of such pictures upon children from five to eight or nine years of age. I once was talking to a distinguished public servant

by the party of my hon. friend he is regarded as very distinguished, and is still in the service of the state-who told me that he did not permit these supplements to be placed in the hands of his young children.
In 1930 or 1931, I forget which, when we dealt with this item we dealt with it as we did for two reasons. The first was that these supplements represent additions to the Sunday newspapers that I do not think the most case hardened member of this committee would regard as being the very best literature for the children on Sunday morning. I have listened to an exposition over the radio based

upon one of these coloured supplements, and while I am not an authority at all I have observed the effect upon children of the reading of them. Take one of these coloured supplements, for instance. It leaves an entirely wrong impression as to the relations between a man and his wife. It places a premium upon fraud, lying and deceit. These two Katzenjammer youngsters of whom you see the pictures are elevated to a position of great importance because of their ability to escape the just retribution of their own misconduct. And so it goes; I could give others as well. There are some, of course, that are quite the opposite, that have some value from the standpoint of teaching children the habits of wild animals and matters of that sort, but after much consideration this item was dealt with as indicated.
The duty we imposed amounted to 15 per cent, 22J per cent and 22J per cent. Now these supplements are to enter free when they come into this country prepared for use as supplements to our newspapers, which was the second point dealt with by my hon. friend for Davenport. The hon. member dealt with that question so fully that I am not going to attempt to repeat what he said, but there is no doubt as to what will be the result in regard to employment. There are weekly newspapers in Canada that print these coloured supplements themselves, but the greater number of them are syndicated from the United States, already printed; they are shipped here in great quantities and then folded in with the Sunday newspapers. There is also another supplement, reproduced on calendered paper-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Rotogravures.

Yes, rotogravures, which also would be covered by this item as it now stands, I take it. I do know that a substantial amount of revenue was derived from that source. I happen to know that one newspaper imported those supplements, printed the name of the paper upon them and added them to the Sunday issues, and that newspaper paid us substantial sums in the way of revenue. In a sense those are educational, in a general way, containing as they do pictures of current events of world wide interest, and broadly speaking I think they are to be commended. But when you get down to the others, I do not know whether Moon Mullins adds greatly to the store of knowledge of young and growing children. I am not an authority upon that-
Mr. EULER; You are pretty familiar with him.

I am. Fortunately I have reached an age when the formative period is past and it is not likely to be very injurious to me. If it were I should think it highly undesirable that I should be here. That, however, is the reason that governed in placing the duties on the items in this schedule.
Then there is the other question. Is it necessary to add to the profits of the Sunday newspapers by supplying employment to people out of Canada in order that Canadians may purchase these works of art under the circumstances indicated? I think not, and I did hope that the government would not attack that item at this time. It is just one more of those unconscious influences that are moulding the character of the next generation. If we look abroad and see the lack of discipline that obtains in some sections of this continent I think we will agree that there was never a moment of greater necessity for the imposition of those safeguards that were thought desirable in days gone by in order to shape, form and mould national character along lines that at least would reflect something of the genius of our civilization, the civilization that was built up by the generations that have now gone to their rest, rather than the idea that man owes no duty to his fellows and that an undisciplined horde constitutes a nation. I think that is a very improper conception; I know it is not shared by the minister, by the government, by the supporters of the government or by any hon. member in this house, but I cannot help thinking of the effect of this change. When we were putting on this duty I explained the matter at great length; as a matter of fact I think I took too much time, but in those days I said that we could not measure unconscious influences. All we can do is speculate, but we do know what the effect has been in some countries. Let me repeat that it cannot be good for youngsters to believe that there is merit in deception and fraud, as many of these pictures indicate, and that the reward of the deception of parents and of a lack of discipline is happiness, satisfaction and pleasure. That is all I have to say about it, but I feel very strongly though I am not directly affected by this change. I believe it is a bad thing for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

With respect to the inserts to which the hon. member referred, may I point out that representations are made to me by those interested in the printing of American magazines in Canada that the privilege of importing inserts
will in some cases at least have the effect of retaining in Canada the printing work of certain magazines, and will also involve work for Canadians in the printing on the other side of a highly artistic insert and also the facing page. Frankly I am not sure myself that it is altogether good to have the printing of all sorts of magazines brought into Canada. I know these things give a certain amount of employment, but there are other factors. Prior to 1930, before the duty was imposed, hon. members will remember how time after time in this house we were exhorted to put on a duty. What for? To keep out literature which was described many times in this house as derogatory to the building of character and as productive of a bad effect all round. In fact samples were produced here from time to time and we were told to impose a tariff in order that our young folk, and older folk too for that matter, should not be exposed to the slimy temptation of this sort of reading matter. Now, everyone knows that the introduction of the tariff did not achieve that end.
No, but we do know that the publishers in Canada struck out of the Canadian editions offensive sections published in their home editions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

We must recognize that. We are hearing about it every day now. I am not inclined seriously to regard the future in that respect, particularly as under the general provisions proposed, of which this is one, the higher type American magazine will have some incentive to continue publication in Canada.

The advantage will not of course apply to those of the cheaper order, because they do not use inserts of the kind described.

I have listened attentively to what the minister has said. During my survey among the printers I found support for item 178, which is already passed, and I am under the impression that the minister is confusing the remarks I made in reference to the last half of 183 with the endorsation he received from the printers of 178. During my survey a number of printers told me they had written to him, or proposed writing to him, in opposition to the last half of 183, whereas I have no doubt that some of them had also written endorsing 178. But in no print shop did I find any sentiment in support of .the last half of 183. That is one reason why I did not rise when 178 was under discussion, because my information from the printers was generally in favour of 178.

I have had opportunity on several occasions of discussing the moral aspect of this matter. The economic side has been thoroughly discussed and explained. We are not interested just now in knowing the amount of revenue that will be received by the government-although heaven knows we need all we can get-but what we are chiefly interested in is to bar out the class of literature which should not come into Canada at all. There are two ways by which it reaches Canada, one through the post office and the other by railway or aeroplane. I should like to know what censorship exists over that class of reading matter. Is there real censorship in the minister's department or the Post Office Department to prevent that class of reading matter from coming in? No matter how high the tariff against it may be, people who are inclined to read that rubbish will pay the price to get it. In the interests of the younger generation it should be barred from the country. I discussed this matter many years ago with Mr. Hocken, who frequently made references to it in the house; I shared his views, and I know the house realizes that this is the greatest service we can render to the younger generation. I should like to know from the minister whether there is a real censorship, and under what department it operates, to keep this class of matter out of Canada.

Item 1201 of schedule C of the customs tariff, which is the schedule of prohibited goods, reads as follows:
Books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious, or of an immoral or indecent character.

This item is administered by the Department of National Revenue, the organization set up in the department being continued just as it has been during the past few years. This matter was dealt with when the estimates of the Department of National Revenue were before the house; but I do not know whether the hon. gentleman was present on that occasion.

How many publications
have been barred, say during the last year?
I would have to get that information.
Does the post office exercise any supervision? As far as I am concerned that is the important point. The question of revenue is secondary.

There is a provision in
the Post Office Act, with which I am not very familiar, but which empowers the Postmaster General to deny the use of the mails to such matter.

I agree with the Minister of Finance that perhaps it is impossible through the tariff to exercise censorship over the publication of certain types of supplements to newspapers and magazines. May I draw his attention, however, to what strikes me as an anomaly in the schedule? Under item 183, the one under discussion, we place on the free list newspapers, supplementary editions and comic and pictorial sections to be inserted. But, under item 473a, printing plates of all kinds for periodical publications enjoying second-class mailing privileges, and matrices, metal bases and copper shells therefor, carry an intermediate duty of per cent and a general duty of 25 per cent. It appears to me that these items represent a contradiction of the principle of tariff making, if I may so describe it. The finished product is admitted free, but the materials with which Canadian firms might and indeed do produce these publications carry a tariff. I am not suggesting that item 473a should be entirely on the free list, but I suggest, as did the hon. member for Davenport, that item 183 ought not to be completely free. I believe there is more in the question of employment than would appear on the surface. Men working in the printing trades in Canada have been having difficult times, just as have men in similar trades in the United States. There is no question about that. There has been a sharp falling off in newspaper circulation and commercial printing, so that printers generally in common with many other classes of workmen have been going through difficult

Customs Tariff
times. It does not appear to me that the admission of comic and pictorial supplements would be any contribution to the consumer of Canada, as is very often argued. In other words there would be no great loss if the present tariff were continued. On the other hand, without any doubt there would be a definite loss in employment. I have listened with care to the minister's views on the point, but I fail to appreciate the force of his argument, because I cannot see how there could possibly be as much printing along the lines he indicated, where partly printed sheets were shipped in and Canadian printers did the remainder of the work. I do not believe there would be anything like as much labour or employment as exists at present where these publications are produced substantially in Canada.
I shall admit frankly that there would be an inconsistency in the position I am now taking if one were dealing with the matter from the point of view taken by the leader of the opposition, because I am suggesting that we should allow matrices to come in under item 473a. That I suggest should be permitted until we are ready to clean house in connection with publications of this kind. On the other hand I should like to urge upon the minister that item 183 be returned to its former position. I have not read the treaty arrangements with the United States, but I do not believe this is one of the items. I do not think our friends to the south of the line would consider that in any sense we had violated the spirit of the treaty; certainly I would not wish that to be the case. It is highly desirable that we should stimulate friendly relations between these two neighbouring countries. But on both sides of the line I am sure it is recognized that where any action affects the employment of its people the country affected should have the right to control its position.
I do not believe anything one can say will alter the situation, but I have no doubt the minister is impressed with the views so happily put forward by the hon. member for Davenport, the leader of the opposition and other hon. members. Is there any regulation in
effect or are any efforts made to prohibit the bringing into Canada from the United States of communist or red literature which is being circulated widely throughout Canada?

This kind of stuff is published in New York, shipped in here almost daily, and distributed throughout the whole of Canada, to the detriment of the youth of the country and Canada generally. It is literature of a type that is opposed to law and order, tends to drag down the best things we have, to -wreck government institutions, and opposes almost everything that is good, and yet it is allowed to be circulated throughout the whole of Canada. In the city I represent handbills and various other types of printed matter, which comes in from the United States, are frequently distributed, usually at night, which is when they do their work, like rats in a hole, carrying on their nefarious work after dark. What is being done to protect Canadians against that kind of rotten literature?

Mr. Chairman, the item in schedule C of the customs tariff which I read a few moments ago in reply to an inquiry of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) prohibits the importation of books, printed paper, drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable, seditious, immoral or indecent oharacter, and if literature arrives at one of the custom houses of Canada and there is any reason for considering it treasonable or seditious, it is held and examined, and perhaps prohibited. As the hon. gentleman will appreciate, there is often disagreement as to whether a publication is of a treasonable or seditious character. What he considers treasonable or seditious might be regarded by one of his colleagues to the left as merely enlightening and educative, and for that reason the Department of National Revenue has difficulty from time to time in making decisions which meet with the approval of everyone. However, if the hon. gentleman will bring to my attention the publications ,he has in mind, or will send them to the office, we will make a ruling on them, and if we decide that they are treasonable or seditious they will be prohibited entry into Canada. But if they come in secretly or illegally, that is something the Department of National Revenue cannot control, and in such an instance would, I suppose be a matter either for the preventive service or for the police of the province in which the publication circulates. There are other provisions for the control of such publications, such as the provisions in the criminal code which prevent the publication of what are called seditious libels.

That is for domestic purposes.

Customs Tariff
Yes, if they are published within the country and delivered by one person to another.
That is not what is meant by that.

Perhaps I am wrong about that, but if they are published in the ordinary sense within the country it is a violation of the terms of one or more sections of the code. I believe also, though I cannot speak with much certainty as to this, that there is a provision in the Post Office Act which enables the Postmaster General to deny the use of the mails to certain types of literature such as the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Wilton) has mentioned.

There cannot be any doubt as to the class of literature I refer to being seditious. It prints "down with the government" and that kind of thing. I do not think there could be any doubt in the mind of any intelligent person that it is seditious. I am of opinion that perhaps it does not all come in regularly through the customs but finds its way through secret channels that have no right to exist, and a closer check-up on the [DOT]part of the officials of the department or by the police responsible could stop it. That kind of stuff is being circulated, I think, in all our cities-I know it is in Hamilton,-and, as I have said, is usually distributed at night. From information I have received I know it is distributed from headquarters in New York not a stone's throw from Times Square, where in a basement they prepare, publish, and send out this rubbish to the various branches of the red element throughout Canada. It seems to me that an effort should be made on the part of the secret service to check-up on this kind of thing which is undermining and against the very best things we have in the country.

My attention was directed not long ago to an editorial in a weekly newspaper published in New York, an old paper, referring to His late Majesty King George V in terms so offensive that no decent British citizen could read it without a feeling of strong resentment. That one editorial of itself would undoubtedly have justified one, had one known of it before hand, in taking steps to prevent that issue from entering Canada. But inasmuch as the newspaper circulates and there is no repetition of anything of that kind, I think we are powerless to deal with the matter. I do not see how under the existing law we could. The minister is more familiar with it than I am, but I could not see any way of dealing with that particular
situation. We could deny the publishers the privileges of the mails as a punishment for a past offence, but that is not the general principle of the law. The article was a most scurrilous one and I will show it to the minister some day. I have never seen anything quite as bad. I wonder what action we can take that will adequately deal with such offences, because we cannot prosecute under the criminal code or any other statute, though we could deny the publishers the mails as a punishment for having thus insulted us. But, as I say, that is not the general principle of the law. I am uncertain on that point and I was going to speak to the minister about it under this item.

I would remind the minister that it is not only from abroad that seditious or immoral literature is circulated in Canada; there is a good deal of such literature originating in this country itself. As regards the latter literature it may be said that we can prosecute, but one of the greatest difficulties is to find out who publishes such matter. About ten years ago, as a private member, I succeeded in getting through the house a bill compelling all publishers to keep a record of those who had employed them to publish any article or pamphlet. The bill went through this house unanimously, the members understanding its purpose; but unfortunately it met an untimely death in the other chamber. I have seen in Canada literature which it would be a disgrace to anyone to read. We had a pretty shrewd idea of the town in which it was published but there was no way of bringing it home to the offenders because we could not find out who had printed it. In drafting the bill to which I have referred I followed the British law, which provides that for a period of six months the printer shall keep a record of all those employing him to publish any article, and if such article is found to be seditious or in any other way undesirable the publisher, as a means of avoiding liability himself, must disclose the identity of those for whom he has printed the offensive matter. There is a good deal of seditious literature published in British Columbia today, and it would be of assistance to the forces of law and order if it were known who published this literature. Sometimes it is actual print and sometimes it takes the form of mimeographed matter, but the law would apply in either case. If the government would introduce a bill, and the leader of the opposition would use his influence in another chamber to get it through, it would help to put a stop to the publication in Canada of such offensive literature.

The feeling is entirely mutual.

It seems to me that we should ask ourselves what machinery we have or can create with respect to publications of that kind. My legal friends tell me that there is a law with respect to the matter about which I have just been speaking, but obviously you must catch your hare before you can cook it, and in this instance it appears impossible to trace the authorship.
The bill which I managed to get passed through this house was simple, because on the pamphlet the name of the person publishing it had to be printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Because he has already committed a greater offence. Since the minister has mentioned this matter I may make a few observations. I agree with him; we should overhaul the law in that regard. There is a magazine that persistently attacks

not only members of this house but others; it does so in the sacred name of liberty and of freedom of speech and of criticism, and it is circulated rather extensively. It is true that one of the proprietors was convicted and sentenced to a term in gaol, but nevertheless the magazine continues to be published. Nothing more libelous or false could be published than some of the references in that publication. I did not know anything about it until I received a letter from someone in British Columbia stating that he had read something in that magazine. I did not know what he meant and I asked him to send it to me. The assertion was that $1,300,000 had been given by a certain interest connected with the Montreal harbour bridge to one of the political parties; that the other political party was sharing equally in the spoils, and that I personally should have been punished because I permitted Gundy to sell bonds to the extent of $19,000,000 when the law said that only $6,000,000 worth could be sold. Obviously that sort of thing greatly incenses people. This gentleman wrote to me saying that he would like to have an explanation. The assertion I have cited was mild compared with other statements in the magazine. I remember someone showing me the document to which the minister has referred, a most scurrilous attack on the hon. gentleman. To write a letter to the newspapers denying this rotten sort of thing is only to provide the publicity which the author seeks.
I fear that the remedy suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would fall far short of adequacy, for the reason that in the very circulation of these mimeographed or printed copies the perpetrators are committing a greater offence than that of failure to indicate the name of the publishers. I am going to be perfectly frank about this. There is among political, parties a habit of rejoicing in being able to circulate information and attacks of this sort, and that is the reason amendments are made to the law. Then we hear the cry of liberty and freedom. Attacks of this kind are not limited to any one party; do not think I am in any sense trying to attribute them to one party. But unless the people of this country are willing and prepared to take some steps to protect their rights, they may find them entirely disappear. That has been the history of other countries. The right is not the right of abuse; it is the right of free criticism. The right of free criticism is entirely distinct from the right of abuse-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One of Mr. Maclean's
last speeches in this house was devoted to this subject.

Was it? I was not in
the house at the time, but I recall his having very strong views about the matter. To mention one instance; take the statements made by Arthur Evans. Yet the province had the right to say whether he should be prosecuted; the province says that he is not to be prosecuted, and that is all there is about it; he goes free. It is true that nine others have been prosecuted and convicted. But this has nothing to do with the great and fundamental principle that if we are going to maintain rights we must enforce the law against those who try to deprive themselves and us of it in the name of liberty and freedom, because freedom does not mean licence, neither does liberty. Attacks of the kind referred to are being made in this country at the present time. I am sure that the very discussion which has taken place this afternoon will be the subject of lampoons and attacks that will be anonymously circulated from one end of the country to the other.

One great argument of the late Mr. Maclean had to do with the administration of the federal system and the weakness of its laws. The laws are passed here but they are put into force by the provinces.
If the provinces take no action the law becomes a dead letter. That- has been the great objection to the federal law as it now exists. As the leader of the opposition has said, at the present time the enforcement of federal laws rests largely with the provinces, and if a province takes no action that is the end of the story. I have often heard discussed in this house whether we should not have an officer, with something of the standing of the Lord Chamberlain in England, who would exercise general censorship all over Canada, and have authority from the dominon and the provinces to control theatres and matters of the kind to which reference has been made. There has always been this controversy between the provinces and the dominion. Of course it is primarily a matter for legal gentlemen to discuss, but undeniably it is one of the weaknesses of our federal system.

If we go too far into censorship there is a danger of falling short of providing the protection that is essentially required. We should keep in mind that probably there is no country in the world where the government is more secure than in Great Britain, and there is no country in the world where freedom of speech and freedom of the press are so strongly established as in the British Isles.
Not that kind of speech.

It seems to me that that fact is proof positive that very little danger need be feared from sedition or seditious utterances, whether by word of mouth or by the printed word. I am no more than any other member in favour of the circulation of what is termed communist or scurrilous literature in so far as it is scurrilous or libelous or misleading. I have had the distinction, which is possibly shared by very few members of this house, of having been opposed in the last election by a communist, so that perhaps I can speak with some little authority on the matter. As regards the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) I think something should be done. I have in mind something that happened in the Ontario provincial election of 1934. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or some adherents of that party published a weekly paper for some few weeks at the beginning of that year. It went out of business, I believe, in February. But in June, during the campaign, an issue of that paper appeared, bundles of which were sent to all the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation committee rooms, although certainly neither the

federation nor any one belonging to it printed or paid for that paper. Those who did so had not the courage to put their signatures on it. They did it in order to mislead the electors. We were not altogether free from that kind of thing in British Columbia during the last election. I think that is of more importance than even seditious literature, because it is misleading and it deceives the very people who should be truthfully informed on the issues of an election. If something could be done to curb that sort of thing I should be glad to support it. But as regards banning things that we are not in favour of, just because we do not like them, I think we should go very carefully in that direction, because what is seditious to-day may not be seditious to-morrow.

Provided, that in no case shall the rate of duty under the intermediate or the general tariff be less than: intermediate tariff, 30 per cent; general tariff, 35 per cent.

Under the
present intermediate tariff, containers enjoyed a protection of li cents a pound. That was not enough for the box makers or the carton manufacturers, so the item was increased to thirty per cent, which was quite a sizeable increase. The old rate under which manufacturers of boxes and cartons operated should be plenty of protection for them. This item is not so favourable to the men who manufacture articles which, in order to sell them, they must put into containers of this kind. It works a handicap on them because the thirty per cent duty almost invariably means thirty per cent additional costs. I have in mind, as relevant to this matter, a particular manufacturing concern that has to buy raw material upon which there is twenty per cent protection, and to put its product into boxes or containers on which there is thirty per 
cent protection. A competing article is brought into Canada in a finished state, in a container, and pays a duty of only 7J per cent. Surely that is manifestly unfair, and I think there should be some way of putting it right.

During the course of some
remarks earlier in the session I drew attention to the fact that certain items of the tariff bore a specific duty, and certain items an ad valorem duty. This is one of the items I had particularly in mind, and I am glad th&t my hon. friend brought up his suggestion, which I want to emphasize. After careful investigation I am firmly convinced that the paper-box manufacturers of this country are overprotected at the present time. With this specific duty their protection was quite adequate at the prices for which paper-boxes and containers were selling when the duty was first imposed. To-day this same duty represents almost fifty per cent. The result is that the people who use these containers and boxes have to pay more than they would otherwise do. I would not favour reducing the duty sufficiently to admit paper-boxes or containers from another country; they can and should be manufactured in Canada. I feel that the Canadian manufacturer of paper-boxes is overprotected at the present time and is taking advantage of that overprotection with the result that the user of that material in Canada, who has to put his finished articles into those boxes, is paying almost fifty per cent more than he would pay if the duty were reduced to normal protection.
In connection with the adjustment of the tariff as a result of the agreement with the United States I have in mind a manufacturer who had the tariff on his finished article reduced by 2J per cent. That does not sound very much, but I can assure the Minister of Finance that it meant a considerable amount to that particular industry. He is a manufacturer selling very close to the line, and when this additional advantage of 2^ per cent was given to his American competitor, in order to keep out the American product he had to reduce his price to the point where he could not make a reasonable profit. On top of that he is forced to pay a high price for containers in which to place his finished product.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance if it would not be possible to make this an ad valorem duty instead of a specific duty, and to make that ad valorem duty twenty-five per cent rather than what it is at the present time. This specific duty raises the price of these paper-boxes made in Canada by almost fifty per cent, and the manufacturers are taking full advantage of that to the detriment of other manufacturers who are forced to use these

containers. So I would ask the minister if he would give some consideration to that suggestion so that these people who have suffered because of the trade agreement with the United States might have their difficulties ameliorated to that extent at least.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Such a wide disparity in value had the effect last year, under a specific duty, of creating an ad valorem range as great as from five per cent to forty per cent. What I bring to the attention of the committee to-day is the result of the investigation by the tariff board, at which representations were made both by the users of all classes of these containers and by the manufacturers. The only change suggested by the tariff board report is an ad valorem rate which will equalize the bearing of the specific rate now in force. The recommendation is as set out in the item, that while the duty should remain at li cents per pound by weight it should not be less than thirty per cent ad valorem.
My hon. friend from Mount Royal and my hon. friend from Lambton-Kent have in mind manufacturers of specific commodities who put them into some type of paper containers. Naturally, in drafting the tariff item, the tariff board had to have in mind the whole range of paperboard and fibre-board containers, and also the whole range of manufacturers using those containers, and I should point out that while I have heard the representations made this afternoon by the two hon. members, I do not think I have had any other complaints. I may have had one or two among the thousands of letters I have received, but there has been nothing 12739-189
which has impressed itself on my mind as a complaint with reference to the finding of the tariff board in connection with this particular item. The commissioner tells me that he knows of none at all. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now that my hon. friend has identified the commodity as the large, heavy corrugated box he has thereby defeated his own argument, for the heavy corrugated type of container is the type to which the thirty per cent ad valorem would never apply, because the weight factor involved would ensure that the specific duty would always produce a rate as high as or higher than the one he has just specified as a minimum. That was all developed before the tariff board. I may point out further that it is the old tariff rate; there is no change there. In fact, under the Canada-United States trade agreement there was a reduction of one-quarter cent a pound in favour of the manufacturer to whom my hon. friend refers. My hon. friend's suggestion of a reduction of the minimum ad valorem to twenty-five per cent would not help his friend, because the duty is now levied upon that particular commodity on a weight basis. Surely there must be a difference in the basis of value for duty between that large corrugated paper container and the little paper container which holds a tube of shaving cream. How could you possibly assess value for duty by the pound on paper containers for tubes of shaving cream as compared with the large corrugated paper container which takes, for example a dozen or score pairs of boots or shoes or things of that sort? That is why after a thorough and rather difficult examination the tariff board reached this conclusion. This very instance demonstrates the value of inquiry by some body outside this committee into matters of this kind. Of course all of us are affected by representations made to us by concerns or individuals. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
When this bill was last before the bouse for second reading I moved the adjournment of the debate for the purpose, as I intimated then, of trying to secure information from the various places where the method suggested by my hon. friend is in force, and also for the purpose of communicating with the attorneys general of the various provinces of Canada, because the administration of justice, including criminal justice, is under the control of the provinces.
We communicated with the five states of the American union where the method of lethal gas for the execution of condemned persons is in practice. These states are: Nevada, where they have had the system since February, 1924; Arizona, since November, 1933; Colorado, since 1934; Wyoming, since 1935; and North Carolina, since the early part of 1935. In every one of these states there is a central place of execution, namely, the main gaol of the state.
The method is not at all a complicated one nor is it expensive. It is administered by the government of the state itself and the guards in these prisons do whatever is necessary to carry out executions. This method does not require the services of any technical expert, for almost any guard in the prison is able to do what is necessary.
As to the humaneness of this method of execution, that of course is a question of point of view; but in those states where it has been

Criminal Code-Death Penalty
in practice the officials claim that it is a far more efficient and a more humane method than the other system. As to whether, as a deterrent, it is as efficient as the other, that again is a matter of opinion.
We also communicated with the various provinces, through the law officers, the attorney general or rather the deputy attorney general in every province, who answered our queries. They are to a large extent reluctant to express their opinions, though most of them would rather favour the change if it were proved to be more efficient and more humane. Some of the provinces would like very much to have only one place of execution. For instance, both the attorney general of New Brunswick and the attorney general of Nova Scotia strongly recommend that instead of having executions carried out in the various gaols in these two provinces they should be carried out at the penitentiary, which is in Dorchester, New Brunswick, for the maritime provinces.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext: It would be very unfair to the inmates of the penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Maybe; that is one of the possible objections to the [DOT]change and it would have to be investigated. I instructed one of the officers of the Department of Justice, Mr. Plaxton, to visit those places in the five states which I have mentioned. He has prepared a report giving all the details and the opinions of physicians who have something to do with executions, and on the whole I must say it is rather favourable to the change. This, however, would involve such a radical departure from the present law and practice in Canada that I am of the opinion that this matter should be thoroughly studied and further investigated, at least until the next session of parliament, so as to give public opinion in the country time to express itself respecting the question' what it would be best for us to do.
Of course, if the change suggested by this bill were aocepted, there would have to be one place of execution in the maritime provinces, one in Quebec and Ontario, and one in the west, and there is the objection to which my right hon. friend has just alluded. Then there is this other fact to be considered. As the situation is to-day, under our law, apart from the exercise of clemency where the federal government has to advise the representative of the crown, the death sentence is executed absolutely independently of anything that this parliament or the federal government may do. The matter is entirely under provincial jurisdiction. The province is re-

sponsible for carrying out the execution, the sheriff in every district being the responsible officer in charge.
There are in certain quarters many delusions as to the law and the practice. In days gone by and even this very year I have received as Minister of Justice letters from persons applying for the position of hangman, such persons evidently believing that it is a federal office; and if there were a vacancy some people would be quite willing to be appointed. We have nothing to do with that. The sheriff of each district where an execution takes place is entirely in charge. He retains the executioner, whoever he may be, and the executioner is not in any way connected with the federal authorities nor is he a federal officer. If a change were made, and if instead of having the executions in every district, they were to take place in the penitentiaries, arrangements of some kind would have to be made if the province were still to be responsible. I admit that I would prefer that the present system, as far as responsibility for carrying out executions is concerned, should remain under the provinces rather than be under the federal authorities, where the exercise or the refusal of clemency lies. I think it is a good thing that these two matters should be under different control.
All these considerations will have to be studied; every phase of the matter will need to be investigated. I would suggest that a committee of parliament should deal with the question, look into every consideration, if necessary hear witnesses, including experts. But obviously that could not be done this session, and I would suggest that my hon. friend withdraw his bill for this year and reintroduce it at the next session of parliament.
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition)':	I am sure we have listened
with great satisfaction to the observations of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), indicating as they do that he has given a great deal of consideration to the subject matter of the measure that has been introduced by the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair). Under our constitutional system this parliament determines what acts constitute crimes, and this parliament awards the punishment for a violation of the statute which it thus makes. It rests with the provincial authorities to carry into effect any sentence that may be imposed, whether it be death or imprisonment or otherwise, but it is for the federal authority, on the one hand, to provide the penitentiaries, and, on the other, for the provinces to provide the gaols in which

Criminal Code-Death Penalty
imprisonment is made. That is one of the anomalies of our constitutional system.
The form which punishment for murder or any other offence punishable with death should take has been a subject matter of discussion, I suppose, ever since there has been law. There are two factors to be considered. One has to do with the punishment, which is determined by this parliament; the other has to do with the effect of that punishment upon society. One is intended to operate as punishment of an offender, the other as a deterrent against the repetition of such acts by other members of society. There is no doubt that the form which punishment takes has been regarded from the earliest dawn of history as important in determining the value of punishment as a deterrent. It will be recalled that in the very early days death was inflicted sometimes through stoning the offender to death, in other cases by beheading the offender. But hanging was always an ignominious form of death. Hence it was that when men in military service were convicted they pleaded that they should not be hanged but that they might be shot, because one was such an ignominious form- of death as compared with the other. My reading induces me to believe that hanging is far, far more effective as a deterrent than any other form of punishment which has been devised. While the putting to death of a convicted criminal by suffocation, by asphyxiation or in a lethal chamber may indeed be a very humane method, with all deference I have to say that it is not humanity we are concerned about in the inflicting of punishment, it is the preservation of society from those who have offended against it, and the method of punishment that we resort to is not to find the most humane method by which to punish the offender, but in the same act to punish and to deter. I frankly say I do not know of any method that we have yet had upon the statute books of any country, that is more calculated to operate as a deterrent than is hanging. Whether we like it or not, that, at least, is the evidence of history, and it cannot lightly be disregarded. It arises from the ignominy that attaches to that form of punishment. For instance, in the days when a prisoner was beheaded, it will be recalled that very frequently the body was put in irons, taken to a near-by tree and suspended there, and left hanging as an example to all who might pass that way as to what was the ultimate reward of the felon. In some cases the bodies were quartered, and they were buried under conditions that we should regard as revolting, as for example, when a stake was driven through the corpse. One who reads
the Calendar of Newgate will find there striking illustrations of the facts to which I allude.
I think we can derive some lesson from what the practice in England has been. There is no country in all the world in which there is a higher regard for law than there is in the British Isles, and to this day the punishment of the man convicted of murder is hanging. We adopted it when we founded our criminal jurisprudence. In one part of the United States they have followed the practice of hanging. I believe that in one state of the union they still shoot the offender, and there are countries in Europe in which the murderer is shot to death. As those will remember who have read a recent book published by the warden of Sing Sing, electrocution was introduced into the United States, as it has been into other states, and it has been found to work satisfactorily. Yet when one reads of it, and realizes the steps that are taken to make it effective, I think one will conclude that the method which is adopted as part of the criminal jurisprudence of Great Britain and is still followed here is the most satisfactory method, having regard to the second branch of the purpose of the execution of a criminal. So, when I heard the Minister of Justice make the observation he did, I felt that he properly reflects public opinion. There is such a thing as a maudlin sentimentality with respect to the criminal that has brought about a condition in society which is not to be desired. It must be recalled that those who are punished for sins against society and for crimes against the law are, in the words of a great authority, like the mad dog or the wild wolf. They are destroyed not because of resentment or because of any feeling of animosity against them, but because, by their conduct and actions, they have made it essential for society to destroy them in order to preserve itself, and in the effort to preserve itself it necessarily must have recourse to methods which sometimes are not, shall I say, the happiest or yet the most pleasant. Therefore I repeat that I heard with much satisfaction the observations of the minister.
I would not for a moment venture to make a suggestion to the hon. member for Wellington North with his wide knowledge as a physician and his earnest desire to save human suffering, but we must never forget the person who was killed. I recall, when we had to deal with capital cases, receiving petitions signed by tens of thousands of people pleading for clemency. The rule that, I think, is the sound one is that if a murderer has been convicted

Criminal Code-Death Penalty
by due process of law the sentence should not be interfered with by the executive, not having seen the witnesses, because you cannot tell the weight that is to be attached to the evidence of witnesss without having seen them, without having observed their demeanour and without being in any way able to appreciate the frankness or otherwise with which the testimony was given. But when we have to consider the question of the method to be pursued we must not forget that the murderer was not very careful about the method he selected to destroy his victim. We must not forget that those about whom we are so solicitous were not solicitous for those whom they destroyed. When they wreaked their vengeance, by murder dark and foul, they were not thinking of the pain they caused or the injury they did; they were not thinking of the sorrow they caused to those who survived. In this age there are always manifestations of our becoming victims of maudlin sentimentality and thinking in terms of the pain and suffering of one whom we are removing from society because of his offences against it, but at the same time I suggest that we should never forget those who have suffered because of the offences which have been committed.
I commend the minister for not endeavouring to change the established system at this time, and for deciding to await some stronger manifestation of public opinion than we have yet seen realizing that a practice which has been followed so satisfactorily in the country where law is more highly respected than in any other part of the world is a method from which we should not lightly depart in Canada, where it has been followed for so long. I am not unmindful of the other difficulties to which the minister has referred, and which are real ones. To establish a central point at which all criminals would be sent from two or three provinces would be to put the provinces to an increased expenditure, and that burden is already great in connection with the administration of criminal justice. In my opinion this would tend to lessen the value of the effect that attaches to the second branch of all punishment, namely as a deterrent against the performance of similar acts by others.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, without going into the matter in any further detail from either the historical or any other standpoint, I must say that I am greatly pleased that the minister has taken the view he has expressed. I cannot but hope that when all the facts have been reviewed by the hon. member for Wellington North, having regard to the

effect that it is always purposed to achieve by punishment, he will agree that, consistent with humane methods and the deterrent effects, hanging has served a great and useful purpose as a method of depriving of life one who has been convicted, usually for taking the life of another. It is true under our criminal code, there are other offences, notably treason and rape, for which death is the punishment, but usually the fact is that death is awarded as a punishment-automatically it is true-when the verdict has been that the accused is guilty of murder. It will be found that in the many years during which hanging has been the punishment imposed for murder in Great Britain and other parts of the British dominions it has been a satisfactory method of taking the life of a human being by process of law, alike for punishment and for deterring others from perpetrating similar acts.

speechtext: All right; all kinds of criminals are either born or made. It used to be considered that there were certain criminal types; there may be; I do not want to go into that. There may be criminal types, as stated some years ago by some outstanding criminologists. If that is the case then we cannot very well blame the criminals; they are criminally insane; we can put them out of the way in the most humane manner possible or shut them up. In my judgment instead of adopting another method of capital punishment we should abolish it altogether; that would be the best way, and that is not maudlin sentiment. In my judgment the great majority of criminals to-day are not bom that way; they are made that, way by social maladjustments.

If some who lightly brush aside these matters would read a little more carefully the history of criminals, they would understand that to a considerable extent criminal instincts 'have not been inherited by these people, but criminal tendencies have been fostered by poor training in childhood and the difficulty later on of finding the way into a satisfactory manner of living in our society as it is to-day. Under those circumstances I urge that it is for us to do one of two things: If law breakers are criminal in type, to take steps to prevent criminals coming into the world. For those who are not bom criminals, the thing to do is to arrange our social affairs so that they may not develop criminal tendencies. That is why I am so often on my feet advocating social changes. I think I am perfectly scientific in doing so. If instead of spending so much in the building of bigger and better penitentiaries, we spent a little more in providing work and recreation and decent surroundings we would not have anything like so many criminals.
The leader of the opposition suggested that society must destroy certain people in order to preserve itself. Of course society must seek to preserve itself; I quite agree that -the statement is true in those general terms. But I submit that if we simply set to work to wipe out a few individuals who 'have proved dangerous to society we are not really curing the social evils which we find about us to-day. Capital punishment may be the last desperate remedy, if you like. But if my reading of history is correct; if we disregard the welfare of any considerable section of the community, it is not very long, as historical time is measured, before those people in some form or another take their revenge on society.

In closing, because I do not want to argue this matter, I want merely to protest against the observations of the leader of the opposition. If we are going to discuss capital punishment at all it seems to me we might

discuss these broader issues as well. If we must resort to capital punishment it is all to the good to see that it is effected in as humane a way as possible. We are not out for vengeance on the poor fellow who has committed the crime. As to vengeance look at some of the photographs being circulated to-day showing the mutilations which took place in Ethiopia, that is if you want to get stirred up in that way, have all the vengeance you like, as in some of the southern lynchings. But surely we do not want that; the leader of the opposition does not want that. If the punishment is to be a deterrent, let it be effected as humanely as possible; place it on a high plane. If certain people may no longer be safely allowed in society and for that reason have to be either put out of life or put away where they can no longer endanger society, let it be done with dignity and mercy.

Last
week in Toronto one of these executions took seventeen minutes. Last year in Montreal a woman had her head torn off. There is a demand in the country to have the present system improved or to get a more humane system.
While this bill is before the house I also wish to register a complaint about an execution last week from which the press were excluded, the first time I have known this to be done. That is contrary to sections 1065, 1066 and 1067 of the criminal code, which relate to the place of execution, the persons who shall be present and the persons who may be present. Publicity is one element of the administration of justice.
Some more humane method should be adopted. The medical council and the judges should be consulted, and probably 'by next year the minister could find a way for Canada to carry out its executions as a federal authority instead of leaving them to the provincial authorities. The government of Canada now seems to be administered from the provincial capitals. Section 1067 relates to the persons who may be present, the latter including any justice for the district, and such relatives of the prisoner or other persons as it seems proper to the sheriff to admit. In this case they were out on the street walking up and down, and the sheriff had no discretion; he was instructed to exclude even the representatives of the four Toronto papers, something never done before. This inhumane method of execution is just another example of the fact that Canada is at t'he rear rank of the procession as far as any effort for law reform is concerned in the British empire to-day.
