I am almost afraid to rise to speak on this question because of its bearing upon our life, and especially our criminal life. Forty years ago I debated this subject, that capital punishment should be abolished, and I have never heard a debating club win which took the side that capital punishment should not be abolished. Invariably the abolition of capital punishment is favoured. The bon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) used the argument against hanging that it was those who carry out the execution who were being punished. I have heard guards, coming out pale-faced after an execution, saying, "God pity men who have to witness a thing like that. I would rather resign my position than have to go through that again." I am not one who believes that hanging, or any mode of execution whatever it may be helps to make our country more law-abiding. I am convinced that the enforcement of law to a great extent depends upon the character and calibre of our judiciary. Our judges and magistrates, and even our lawyers represent the enforcement of law and order in Canada.
I am convinced that criminals are not born; they are made. Otherwise I could not preach the old gospel, and neither could I take part in constructing laws for the betterment of society. If I believed that criminals were born, not made, then I would lean towards the old doctrine of fatalism. I am convinced, too, that criminals might be used in a way better than that of simply putting them out of business by coarse measures. Medical science is always exploring and attempting to find ways to help humanity. I believe it would foe a good thing if a person convicted of foul murder might have his life used for experimental purposes, so that young doctors could conduct their experiments for the betterment of humanity.
Hanging is perhaps the worst form of execution. When we condemn a vile murderer we often hear the statement that hanging is too good for him. But as I said, the form of execution does not help in the administration of justice. We like to live in the Old Testament days and observe the principle of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But we are not living in Old Testament times, times when things were at a standstill. We are living in a new day when we regard human life as sacred. If a criminal is put out of existence, then he is just in hell a little sooner than otherwise.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF HANGING AS DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to a certain extent I believe I am qualified to speak authoritatively on the subject of hanging, not because I was ever hanged, or expect to be, but because it was my unfortunate duty on one occasion some years ago, while engaged in newspaper work, to witness a hanging. I assure you, sir, that any person who has witnessed a legalized killing of a human being by the method of hanging would have no desire to see a second one.
Even if the present system of hanging were continued there are certain conditions surrounding it which I suggest should be eliminated. At the hanging to which I refer the prisoner was brought from his cell and paraded from that point to the place of execution, during which time he passed his own open grave. That in itself was perhaps worse than the actual hanging. I know it seemed to take more out of the condemned man than did even the ascension to the scaffold and the actual hanging.
Hanging as I have known it from personal experience is cruel, barbarous and everything it should not be. While I am not suggesting that we should discard the death penalty, the fact is that we are in a complex situation when we attempt to follow the divine law which stipulates a life for a life, but reject the law which says, "Thou shalt not kill." However, as long as we take a life for a life I suggest that we should do it along lines no worse than we would adopt towards animals. The society for the prevention of cruelty to dumb animals surrounds its work with more humanity than do we, as human beings, in the disposal of human lives by hanging.
For example, if a man were to hang a dog I have no doubt public sentiment would rise in indignation and protest strenuously against his action. I should not be surprised if he were brought before a court and fined for cruelty to animals. At the hanging it was my unfortunate duty to witness the man was not pronounced dead until fourteen minutes after he had been dropped. Quite recently I read of a hanging in Toronto where seventeen minutes elapsed before the death pronouncement was given. I have before me a clipping from a Kitchener newspaper stating that a man had been fined in court for cruelty to chickens. These chickens had been deformed in some way, and he had not given them the proper attention.
The laws under which human society functions give greater protection to dumb animals than we as a government give to the men whom we condemn to death. If a man breaks

Criminal Code-Death Penalty
a law and as a result is condemned to be hanged, then that is the law of the land, but I have never been able to believe that the law has any right to add to that man's torture further than putting him to death, in whatever way is decided. As I said before, when bodies are not claimed by relatives and are buried in the courtyard or gaol yard prisoners are marched past their open graves. That in itself at least needs correction even though the present system remains. The system of putting human beings to death by hanging is barbarous; it is antiquated; it is cruel, and we as modern people trying to live up to modern conditions, priding ourselves on being a nation of modern people with modern ideas, still continue to follow this barbarous method of putting men to death by hanging when we have the evidence before us that it takes from fourteen to seventeen minutes, and sometimes longer, after the hanging before death is pronounced. As I said before, anyone who has ever witnessed the legalized killing of a human being by hanging will forever after be opposed to it on the ground of common humanity as something inhuman, barbarous, and not in keeping with modern civilization.
I have before me another clipping here, to the effect that a man in Toronto kept his dog in the basement of his house; the humane society, believing that that was not just the proper place to keep a dog, had the man brought into court where a conviction was registered against him on the charge of cruelty to animals, and he paid a fine. Every possible precaution is taken to protect dumb animals from suffering, to prevent human beings from inflicting on them torture of any kind, and still we as a people and as a government stand by and say nothing while the state puts men to death by a method that inflicts possibly more torture than any other yet invented. Whatever system is adopted it seems to me that there are several ways of executing the death sentence which would be more humane and more in keeping with modern conditions than by putting men to death by legalized killing through hanging.
I want to put myself on record as being absolutely opposed to the system of killing by hanging. So long as the laws of this land demand a life for a life, the death sentence should be executed in at least a humane way, in a way that is as nearly painless as possible, and not surrounded with any of the gruesome details which always accompany death by hanging.

Mr. Speaker, at the very outset I want to make it plain that I realize that the legally trained mind probably approaches this problem from

a very different viewpoint from that of the theologian as illustrated by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) or from that of the medical man.
The point at issue in this bill is not the abolition of the death penalty. The point is: Shall we substitute the lethal chamber for hanging? The greatest deterrent to crime in any country is the certainty of prosecution if crime is committed, and the certainty of punishment if the prisoner is convicted on that prosecution. Once a man has been convicted of murder the death penalty must be imposed, and, as I stated, the point in this bill is not as to whether we shall have the death penalty, but as to the method by which the convicted criminal shall be put to death.
A considerable number of the members of this house dwelt upon the fact that life was not pronounced extinct for a given number of minutes after the criminal in question was hanged, but if we are to consider this matter on the basis of humanity the question as to how long a time may elapse between the actual dropping through the trap in a hanging and the pronouncement by a medical man of life being extinct has nothing whatever to do with the matter. What we are interested in is: How long does it take from the moment the criminal is taken from his cell, knowing certainly that he is going to be hanged, until unconsciousness is produced? I asked both the mover (Mr. Blair) and the seconder (Mr. Howden) of the bill as medical men, when they moved and seconded this bill, if they would tell me the length of time required to produce unconsciousness from the moment the man drops through the trap and the neck is broken, which we believe is the method by which hanging is executed, thereby putting upon the spinal column a pressure which in turn produces unconsciousness. But neither gentleman saw fit to answer that question. As against that I asked the length of time which elapsed from the time a condemned murderer is taken from his cell until unconsciousness is produced in a lethal chamber.

Will the minister say what the policy of the department is in regard to defence?

That is a difficult question to answer, but I may tell the hon. gentleman at once that the policy of the department is not necessarily a policy that changes with a change of administration. Discussing the supplementary estimates of the department the other day, I said that the policy of the department was naturally and essentially concerned with the defence of the dominion. Those who have acted as technical advisers for many years and who have studied the question have said that the defence of Canada is concerned with four possible developments. In the first place there is the defence of our own coasts; second, the defence of our neutrality in the event of war between other nations; third, the possibility, which I hope is a very remote one, of Canada being compelled at any time to dispatch an expeditionary force in order to fulfil her obligations under the terms of the covenant of the league, and in the fourth place the possible dispatch of an expeditionary force consequent upon any contingent developments in relation to our position in the British commonwealth. In my own judgment, however, the position of the defence forces of Canada comes within the first two: that is, with reference to policies which should be adopted for the defence of our own coasts if necessary, and, second, for the defence of our neutrality, the defending of focal points of trade routes in case of war between other nations. Increase the grant, and get more.

I have been wondering what is the justification for this expenditure. As one who has had considerable experience in charge of institutions where this particular work is being done, I believe that it is one of the most wasteful expenditures the dominion is making at the present time. As a matter of fact, in practically all the provinces and practically all classes of schools, physical training is given on more or less scientific principles, following particularly the Swedish and British systems. The training that cadets get has, it seems to me, very little to commend it. It is entirely, shall I say, supplementary, and is not regarded in some quarters as anything but a method of obtaining a grant from the federal government. Of course an effort is made on the day that an inspection is held to parade as many boys as possible, and to give them, shortly before, a certain amount of military training. But in my opinion the boys and girls who are receiving physical training apart altogether from military training are more thoroughly trained physically than could possibly be done through cadet drill. If the justification of this work is that you are training boys to participate in war on some future occasion.
that of course is a point of view which one can understand, but so frequently we are told the justification is that it helps the youth of the country to develop physique. As a matter of fact it does nothing of the kind. Physical training can be well looked after under the system in vogue in most provinces and in most schools, apart altogether from military drill. I would also point out that the poorest possible kind of physical drill is the military drill. It is not balanced. About all it requires is a blind and unreasoning obedience to orders which are given in rather a crisp and curt manner. In my opinion this does not tend to breed in an individual initiative and self-reliance; I think it does exactly the opposite.
There is another feature that I should like to draw to the attention of the house. In certain places military drill or cadet drill is made more or less compulsory. Boys whose parents are opposed to militarism are more or less forced either to take cadet drill or to suffer certain indignities. If I may recount my own experience, I have a son who has just attained his majority. He has never taken military drill; I have always objected to it. Yet in one of the collegiates in the city in which I live, that boy day after day was taken into the basement when the drill was being held and compelled to sit on the form and watch the other boys. In an institution of which I was the head a few years ago definite instructions were given to me that I was not -to excuse boys from military drill unless they were physically unfit to take part in any form of drill. I may say that I personally challenged that ruling; my views were upheld by the Saskatchewan Department of Education, and the order was nullified. Nevertheless pressure is placed upon boys to take this cadet drill. In my opinion the grant that we are making for this purpose might be placed somewhere else in the estimates. If it is looked upon as being necessary for the development of our youth it could be utilized much more beneficially in the encouragement of other forms of physical exercise that are non-military and better balanced, and in the promotion of good sportsmanship in the playing fields of our schools, where, after all, the best kind of sportsmanship is developed.

All I desire to say is that in my humble opinion this grant of $150,000 is worth two or three times what it costs in encouraging a spirit of loyalty to king and country in the hearts of our youth.

I rise to a point of order. I should like to correct that statement; I did nothing of the kind. As a matter of fact, owing to my parents seeing fit to give me an unusual first name it appeared on the ballot paper in that way. When that name was given me I was too young to make an effective protest.

I stand corrected. I have in my hand the official list of candidates, and there I find the name "Major." It strikes me that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar might have been well advised to steer clear of that unfortunate mistake, because I have not the least doubt that it won him very many votes. Speaking in my own behalf, and remembering the words of my hon. friend as to crisp and curt pronouncements, I have had the pleasure of listening to many crisp and very curt pronouncements by the hon. member, and I have admired them. I felt that the discipline, both mental and physical, which can be inculcated in no way as well as by military training, must have been enjoyed by the hon. member. For my own part I should like to say that I think this very moderate estimate is more than justified, and I should like to vote in favour of it.

Might I make just one observation in reply to the remarks of the hon. gentleman who just sat down, first with reference to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar securing any votes because of his Christian name. It happens that I campaigned in the hon. gentleman's constituency, and I am quite convinced that his people know him to be a confirmed pacifist, so they would not be likely to confuse his Christian name with any military title.
Now I should like to say a word with reference to the value of cadet training. For the past fifteen years I have been connected with boys' work in one form or another. I was a member of the cadet corps and later, for a number of years, a member of the militia. I have had contact with the boy scout movement, and the trail ranger and tuxis movement, as well as with a number of athletic clubs in different parts of western Canada, and if the object of this vote is merely the physical development of the youth of Canada, the encouragement of sportsmanship, loyalty and all those things we like

to term Canadian, we could spend the money to much better advantage in a number of boys' movements such as boy scout work or athletic clubs rather than cadet training which, as has been said already, in a great many instances is spasmodic and irregular and often headed by men not altogether trained in the handling of young boys. I think this is simply a waste of money, spent as it is now.

Whether or not it is true, it is being said that when teachers in training at the normal schools get their certificates as physical training instructors the certificates are from the Department of National Defence. I should like to know whether or not that is so.
I am informed that is correct.

I think it is queer that the certificates should come from that department. Year after year-I really think this is the eleventh or twelfth time-I have argued at length and in detail against military training in schools, and I do not prospose to do so again. I am glad that other people who have come to the house are doing this, so I do not need to. However, I do feel that this $150

It might as well be $150, for all the good it does. I think this item should be deleted. I do not think cadet training is good physical training. I think it is poor mental training, and I believe the only kind of discipline that is of any use is self-discipline rather than the kind which comes from commands that are barked out. In looking over the figures a few moments ago I noticed that most of the cadets are being trained in the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. This training is not taken very seriously in any other part of Canada. I think there is a feeling throughout the country against this vote and against this method of physical training. I think the hon. member for Weyburn was quite right when he said that if we are to spend $150,000 on what we call physical training it should be spent in some other way. Let us vote it through the departments of education of the provinces and let it be spent for really physical training.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to this amendment and to the item, because I do not wish to have to make two speeches,

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
I may say that I have seen this vote for cadet services cut down from 3500,000 to $150,000, which means that the government has accepted the policy of the pacifists in and out of this house. Formerly I belonged to a board of education. The last generation in the city from which I come were trained in the cadet movement, and if you look over the reports which I have seen with regard to these cadet services you will find that it is not a military organization any more than the boy scouts or the girl guides. It does help to imbue the cadet with qualities which to-day are necessary for success in life. Look over the gaols and prisons of this country to-day; look at the findings of judges, magistrates and juries throughout this country as to the lack of home training, discipline and training generally for the youth of to-day, and you will see. the need for training of this kind. In the old days juvenile courts were never heard of. I do not like to disagree with the most estimable lady member for Grey-Bruce, but I am heartily in accord with this vote. I am sorry to see the board of education in Toronto, composed of pacifists, and everybody there who calls himself a doctor, oppose the cadet movement; the result has been that this movement has been practically abolished in that city, where they spend 311,000,000 or $12,000,000 on education.
What is this movement? We never would have had a militia in this country had it not been for the 'v.det movement. The history of the militia of Canada is wrapped up with the cadets and the schools. The qualities necessary for success in life are those which the average cadet develops, namely self-control, courtesy, manliness, discipline, love of country. As Pope says, "Worth makes the man." These qualities were fostered by the cadet movement. It was no more military than the show the board of education of Toronto put on last month at the arena, on, I am sorry to say Holy Thursday, a religious day. They dropped the cadet movement; it is now limited to the high schools and after hours; yet they put on a show ten times more military and far more objectionable than anything done under the cadet movement. The ground of the objection to this vote is the principle of pacifism. Militia and defence are necessary. It was the armed strength of the barons that made magna charta possible. The disarmament of the free is the tyrant's chance, now as in the days of King John and as in the case of Ethiopia. If this country wants to abolish the militia altogether the minister's department might as well be closed up. These 12739-190
estimates used to be about two and a half times this amount when I first came to the house. As one who has taken a great deal of interest in education I am absolutely opposed to dropping the cadet movement for some of the fads and frills in the public school system of this country to-day, and Ontario especially, where the cadet movement has been abolished and the board of education and others are shouting pacifism from the housetops.
People are relying upon the League of Nations; the League of Nations is dead and so is Locarno, a mass of ruins. We see the absolute failure of Woodrow Wilson's policy; fifteen years of his open diplomacy has placed our empire in a defenceless state. If the Italian army had come west up the St. Lawrence instead of going south to Ethiopia we should have known the necessity of a proper defence force. Here we are spending four and a half million dollars on the League of Nations, sending a deputation away next week, advisers and advisers to advisers, and all these people over there doing nothing on a joy ride. When the reports are made we never see them, but here hon. members object to a small vote of $150,000 for all the schools of this country from Vancouver to Halifax. The step taken of abolishing the cadets, by the board of education of Toronto is a mistake, a wrong step, and in the juvenile courts all over this country we see the results of the folly involved. I was at the Union station a few days ago and saw twenty-one young people brought back in custody from new Ontario, the district where some hon. members went last weekend. Formerly these young people would have been cadets, but this cadet work has been cut out during the last three or four years with the result that they have not had this training. Some of their parents are on relief; the boys did not want to hang round the house, so they went north to new Ontario to try to find jobs. Unable to get jobs they are cast into gaol as vagrants.
Two or three years ago they substituted for the cadets at the empire day exercises, what? They brought little children, six, seven and eight years of age, to the exhibition grounds; some of them had to walk and ride several miles. They were brought there to a dusty track and left there for hours, instead of having a proper cadet service in the schools and on the property to look after them. From what I have seen of this cadet movement it is not in any sense a military movement, but it teaches the qualities which I have named. I hope it will be restored; it will have to be if we are to have any better



Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
discipline in the land. To-day there is not the discipline such as there was when you, Mr. Chairman, and I went to school. To-day the militia vote is so cut, that about all we have left to defend us, if the enemy came to our gates, is the girl guides and the boy scouts. I cannot understand what objection there is to this vote. It is so little, I do not think the city of Toronto gets anything from it, although it. contributes over $80,000,000 to the revenue of this country. I do not see the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) here; he was here a few minutes ago. He was one of the founders of the splendid Irish regiment and he knows how cadet training helps the initiative. The Irish race know what discipline is. They used to have a cadet corps in his unit; I do not think they have it now, but I know that if cadet services were restored we would have a lot more discipline than we have to-day.
One has just to read the reports of inspectors of the penal institutions of this country to see the need for this training. I had before me the reports in connection with another bill. If you cut out the cadet services altogether you destroy one of the best agencies for the inculcation, in the young people attending school, of the qualities I have named, qualities which are proper and necessary for success in life to-day as they were in the last generation. This matter has been discussed by the Ontario educational association, and many are thinking that we should get back to the old system, instead of substituting for it dances, physical exercises, acrobatic events, and so forth. I am not opposed to those things; they are proper under modern conditions, but they have taken forms which are far more military than were the cadet activities.
I hope the minister will next year have the opinions of various school boards and boards of education throughout the country, and will have cadet services restored. Then the militia will have a chance. This will be an economy in the long run, because there is no doubt that the average cadet went into the militia. The back-bone of the regiments in Toronto was a cadet movement in our city schools. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Baker) was a cadet, and wore a uniform. He can tell us about the advantages of the cadet movement that has been abolished in public and high schools. I know many high school teachers in the city of Toronto. I was on the school board for some years, and I have learned of no agency which has contributed more to athletic and other developments than has the old system of cadet training which has been in operation for the last generation.

I do not wish to add to the remarks of the hon. member for Broadview, who has immediately preceded me, but if I were moving an amendment-and I shall not do so, because I know it would be lost-I would move not to reduce the amount to one dollar but to double it to $300,000.

It is not my intention to say very much, but I must say that many speakers this evening have not spoken from practical experience. I speak from experience, because I have raised three boys to manhood. They have taken their places in the world as good, decent, law-abiding, middle-class citizens, the best class we have. Each of those boys had semi-military training and I attribute the fact that my boys have done comfortably well in the world to the fact that they were given semi-military training and discipline. With the cadet movement not only did they obtain military training, but they had manual training and development of the muscles of their bodies. They were brought up to respect their elders and to obey promptly and quickly when they were spoken to, far more so, I believe, than the boys and girls of to-day who do not have the opportunity of that training.
If I were to move an amendment I would not only double, but treble the vote. The future of Canada depends upon the boys and girls of to-day and those boys and girls, the men and women of the future, will be only what we make them, with the discipline which we can enforce.
Does this vote include public and high school cadets only, or does it also include the Canadian officers training corps in the universities?
It does not include the officers training corps.
Is there a separate vote for the Canadian officers training corps?

They
come under the general training vote.

I support the amendment, because from my experience I have learned that the expenditure of public money under the present method of cadet training is of no practical value. I have had experience in cadet corps, and have had an opportunity of comparing the results of cadet training with those of a proper system of physical training under other institutions. I have found that the results achieved under an up to date method of physical training are much greater. When one considers the problem from the

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
standpoint of national defence, he must conclude that physical training makes a greater contribution towards effective defence.
Time and again eminent military authorities have said that above all other considerations it is necessary to establish the correct physical training and development of our youth. I am not advancing my own opinions on this occasion, because the subject has been discussed by various organizations interested in educational problems. I refer to home and school federations, clubs and the like. There is a great body of opinion firmly opposed to cadet training, after careful observation of the results achieved.
I also refer to the opinion expressed by organized ex-service men. I had occasion to attend a conference of ex-service men, a representative body on the lower mainland of British Columbia. In that body were former officers, as well as men from the ranks. They examined the problem carefully and declared themselves as being opposed to cadet training because it has no practical value. They saw the boys under the command of instructors on the school grounds; they saw them controlled by antiquated drill methods, achieving no information of value in regard to military training, and certainly no training conductive to the true spirit of discipline, but rather the old spirit of discipline which tends to rob the young man of initiative and resourcefulness. Above all they saw that no definite effort was being made to develop these young men physically. The handling of a rifle or the obedience to words of command issued by a drill instructor trained in old methods has no definite value from the standpoint of physical training.
Those who have kept abreast of the requirements of military training to-day will realize that the methods employed are inadequate, and by no stretch of the imagination could it be said that these young men are being properly prepared for any military eventuality. Rather the spirit of the organization of cadet training is to place before them an entirely false ideal of militarism, something which constitutes a definite appeal to their vanity and is unsound in its very conception.
I suggest that at this time, when the country is confronted with such grave problems of youth, it is quite unnecessary to vote even $150,000 for cadet purposes. Rather I would suggest that, in so far as they are available, the moneys should be spent along educational and physical lines, which would more effectively cope with the serious problems of our times.

Cadet training is no longer being carried on in that community, and the federal government does not make any contribution to it.
It will be recalled that this house was provided with evidence from some of the provinces to the effect that cadet training was being reduced, because it must be recalled that in connection with cadet training the schools and others responsible for its promotion are largely under provincial control. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: After the debates in .this house years ago, in which my hon. friend had almost convinced me, as she does every time she speaks, I met a personal friend of mine who is a member of the council of a very large educational institution in the province of Quebec, where they have a 'large number of cadets in training, and I asked him why they were strong for it. He said, "Because we have come to the conclusion that it is the 'best possible method of recreation, sport and physical training at the same time." Cadet training is very popular in all the educational institutions in the province of Quebec, and I can assure my hon. friend that if it were really in t/he nature of a military organization, as it is sometimes described in the house, some of the institutions I know would have quit cadet training long ago.

Mr. Chairman, though I have remained silent through several sessions when this question has been up for discussion, the apparent widening support for the cessation of cadet training in this country makes it incumbent upon me to express my views. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has pointed out to the committee, if I interpreted him correctly, that cadet training produces nothing but a blind and unreasoning obedience and is stultifying to the intellect of the youth of Canada. I would suggest to the hon. member that if he would like to see a demonstration he should go and watch a cadet corps drill in any ^ industrial school or in any institution in this country where boys of feeble mind are put, and then go to one of the schools where there is a cadet corps of normal boys. I aim confident that the difference in their behaviour, in their snappiness and esprit de corps, will convince the hon. gentleman that his conclusion is not well founded.

Would he not know
that without seeing their military training?

He might not have known
it in view of his statement that military training merely produces a blind and unreasoning obedience. I suggest that it takes intelligence and ability and a rapid communication between the mind and the muscles through the sensory nerves to make a well drilled and snappy cadet corps.
I do not support cadet training because -of any aspect of physical training. To me that is a mere incident. I put it upon much higher ground. In my opinion every Canadian citizen owes a duty at all times to serve the state in any capacity in which he reasonably can, and in times of war every Canadian citizen in my judgment owes a duty to the state to bear arms, if necessary, in its defence if he is physically able to do so. If that premise is sound, then I ask: Why not train our youth so that in case of necessity for defence they are efficiently and adequately equipped to render the best possible service to this country? No one desires more than I to avoid war, but I could not help admiring the sentiment which I heard expressed just last Sunday. I happened to be standing watching the garrison parade in the city of Toronto. Next to me was standing a mother, and as her boy went by in a cadet corps in the garrison parade she was affected, and her eyes filled with tears. I passed a remark that it was regrettable that in this world to-day we have nations which were apparently seeking to create war, and that this boy who was being well and efficiently trained might

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
have to serve the country. Her reply was, "How much better I would feel to have him serve than to have him a coward and not be willing to go." I am not expressing a maudlin sentiment; I am expressing a sentiment that, I think, should permeate the heart of every Canadian citizen. I have the greatest respect for those hon. members and any others who may hold views that we should not have military training, be it in the form of a cadet corps or a volunteer militia, but so far as I am concerned my only regret is that, if $150,000 is not sufficient to train every boy in this country who wants to be a cadet, we are not voting more money for that purpose. I have never been able to see where training a boy to bear arms, if necessary, makes him belligerent or warlike. I sincerely trust that there will not be reductions in this grant. Having regard to our recent experiences as to how ineffective a nation or a group of nations may be in preventing war unless they are prepared to back up their reasonable requests, it does seem to me that the best thing Canada can do is to have as many boys and men as possible trained in military manoeuvres and to bear arms, if necessary.

I believe it was understood there was to be a vote and hon. gentlemen flocked in and are disappointed because they think I am going to make a speech. I am not going to make a speech but I want to make one or two remarks. I would reaffirm that the reason we are opposed to war is that we believe it is ineffective. It would be disastrous to our country. And the reason we are opposed to these estimates is that we believe they are absolutely wasteful expenditures and valueless to effect the purpose they have in view, namely, the defence of Canada. I shall speak of that later in the evening or later in the discussion of these estimates. The suggestion is made by the hon. member for York South that every citizen if he were really a good one, should be prepared to bear arms. Some of us do not regard that as the only mark of good citizenship.
I did not say that or anything like it.
Some of us believe that citizenship may be exhibited in a better way than that. Again, the hon. member for York South, referring to an old mother watching a parade-
I did not say old.
Well, a mother watching a parade. She said that she would rather have her son serve than have him a coward, not being willing to go.
Hear, hear.

Somebody says,
"hear, hear." Well, it was the implication contained in that statement that I want to speak of. I resent it. The alternative to being willing to go to the front seems to be that one should appear to be a coward. I do not think that is the alternative at all. Other members have risen in their places and spoken about what their boys owe to military training. I have every reason to congratulate them upon their pride in their children, but some of us who have families have refused to allow our boys to take cadet training, and we do not think that they are inferior, I will not say to the sons of those who have spoken, but to other boys in the community. Surely we should be able to get through a debate of this kind without putting alternatives that are not true. I resent, and a great many weople across the country resent, the idea 
that if a man does not want to go and fight he is necessarily a coward. I should hate to be a coward, but if another war broke out I should hope that not one of my boys would go to fight-and I do not want them to be cowards. I believe they may serve their country in better ways than by going, as a great many went, in my judgment unfortunately, to the battlefields of Europe, where they perished. I do not for one moment deny their heroism; I do not deny their idealism; I think it was magnificent. But I say that there may be heroism and idealism along another line which personally I think is more intelligent.

I was just going to say that I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver North in regard to the danger of placing weapons, under any cir-

cumstanees, in the hands of people who are not trained in their use. Only to-night I was reading the report of the royal commission which inquired into the relief riots in Regina last July 1, and apparently to a very large extent that regrettable incident was due not to the issuing of lethal weapons to certain people but to a mistake in connection with the blowing of a whistle. So it will be seen how easy it is, in the midst of excitement, for someone to commit some overt act, and weapons in the hands of municipal police, for example, who are not particularly trained in their use, may become a danger to the community.

With respect to that matter it will be recalled that the commissioners found that it was subsequently, when the strikers moved off to another part of the community, that the disaster occurred to which attention has been directed. But it must not be forgotten that when the riot act is read certain consequences follow, and if the police of the country cannot be regarded as sufficiently trained to receive weapons why do they carry them around the cities every day? I do not know why, but they do. Policemen in the cities and everywhere are armed at night. To say that they are the only people who should receive -these arms would- be, in my judgment, to make the discretion one based upon sound intelligence, shall I say, for the district officer commanding can only supply weapons to (a) mounted police, (b) provincial police and (c) city police, all of whom are by law' permitted to and do in fact carry arms.

Some misunderstanding may arise with regard -to the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition, particularly in connection with his reference to the reading of the riot act. That was one of the unfortunate features of the whole Regina situation on that occasion. I do not know whether the government is aware of -this fact, but the riot act wTas never read and the warning was never given. I am not placing blame upon anyone, but I just want to make it clear that in that instance the riot act was not read and- no warning was given.

That was not the point. The point was that the strikers had dispersed from their immediate location and moved to another place. The commissioners say that w'hatever justification may have existed in the first instance -because of the misunderstanding of the whistle blasts, there can be no justification for what took place afterwards.
They make that perfectly clear, and they say that at the pavilion which the strikers had abandoned there were found the staffs which apparently they had intended to use for the purpose of bashing the heads of those who might be endeavouring to enforce law and order. The question of the riot act being read did not arise at all, because -these officers had warrants for the arrest of named people, and it was in the execution of that duty that the incident happened. A mistake by some policemen regarding a whistle brought about some measure of confusion, but the commission said that whatever might have been the confusion at this point there was no justification for what happened over at the other point when an attack was made upon the police by those who were subsequently found to be responsible for what took place.

I did not rise to
precipitate a debate on this subject this evening, particularly since I have no doubt that very few members of the house have had an opportunity of reading the report of the commission, so I do not think it would be fair to discuss the matter under this item, nor would it be in order to do so. But I should like to point out that in this instance the riot act was not read, and I think the right hon. leader of the opposition has either misread the report or has been misinformed regarding several matters in connection with it. When the proper time comes perhaps we can discuss this matter in more detail.
I do not propose to discuss the matter raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition-
I did not raise it. It was raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.

Quite so; I meant the statement made by the right hon. gentleman. This is not the time or place to discuss the matter, but I do not think his remarks should be allowed to pass without its being said that the police were not attacked by the men. On this point I notice in the general orders tabled by the minister that rifle associations are being formed and that the men who join these rifle associations must

I have in mind the frequent admonitions by the Minister of Finance that parliament must exercise the strictest economy; yet on the main estimates the total to foe appropriated for the Department of National Defence, including the cost of buildings provided for under other headings, is something like $19,000,000. That does not include the items in the supplementary estimates. This is probably the third highest sum in the departmental expenditures. There is an increase in this year's expenditure in the main estimates of something like $1,779,000-
It is

I accept the correction gladly. I think it is high time we did some plain speaking about the manner in which public money is expended by the Department of National Defence, having in mind particularly the purpose of this expenditure as outlined by the minister. It is not many years ago since certain high officers attached to the British war office recommended drastic reorganization of the Canadian Department of National Defence. As far as I have been able to discover no steps have been taken to undertake such reorganization.
My hon. friend is scarcely correct in that. It is in process of being effected at the present time.
Under whose recommendation is the reorganization being undertaken?

The reorganization of the militia has been under consideration for a number of years. The request for the reorganization became definite in 1932; it was submitted to a subcommittee

Supply-National Defence
of the former government in 1933, because Canada at that time was making certain representations to the disarmament conference in Europe, and the suggestion was made that the strength of our militia forces should be reduced from the post-war figure of eleven infantry and four cavalry divisions to a composite strength of six infantry divisions and one cavalry. That recommendation has been endorsed by all the militia organizations, the defence association, the Canadian infantry association, the artillery association and, I think, every arm of the service, all these voluntary officers, men who have been giving such wonderful service to the militia of Canada. So far the full strength of what is known as the peace establishment has been reduced from a personnel of 135,000 to about 90,000. The actual strength of the nonpermanent active militia is 48,761 as already stated. So far not very much has actually been accomplished along this line, but certain small units have been joined together and reorganization effected. The general policy will be to proceed with reorganization as soon as practicable.

Nevertheless in these times of stress we are asked to vote this enormous sum, without any definite assurance that the purpose for which the expenditure is being made will be fully carried out. We have a headquarters staff here, some seventeen staff officers receiving salaries in excess of $96,000 in the aggregate. We have a number of military districts, each taking large sums of money for their upkeep. We have across Canada something like forty-four units of the non-permanent militia, some 5,643 officers for 36,368 men. According to the last report of the late Sir Arthur Currie with regard to the war establishments, in 1918 there was one officer for every twenty-four men. In the present Canadian establishment we have one officer for every seven men, and for the period of training in camp one officer for every five men. That, I think, has created the general impression in this country that much of this expenditure is devoted merely to the upkeep of a small military aristocracy, and it is difficult to discover what useful purposes they serve, either in providing defence measures for Canada or in making proper preparation for the future. I suggest that the time has come for drastic reorganization of this branch, and that we are not justified at this time in voting the expenditure suggested.
For that reason I move an amendment, seconded by Mr. Taylor (Nanaimo) as follows:
That vote No. 69 for the non-permanent active militia be reduced by the sum of $1,000,000.

I have only one word to say. Probably my hon. friend was not aware that this vote was reduced from last year. I informed him of the reduction effected. I think the committee should not accept his statement that these militia officers constitute a military aristocracy. I know no finer body of men in Canada than these who throughout the year give up four or five nights a week of their leisure and personal pleasure to training the youth of the dominion. There is no suggestion of a military aristocracy about these men. My hon. friend may be confusing the men who have made this their life work with those who are making this permanent contribution to the training of Canadian youth. Some of our unemployed in Winnipeg and Vancouver are among the finest boys we have in the militia. The boys in relief camps joined the militia, took drill and did wonderful service, and I say that is not constituting a military aristocracy or autocracy. They were Canadians binding themselves together in a proper way. There is another thing I want to tell the hon. member, and it is that year after year these militia officers have made contributions to help the men in training camps, because the allowance in the vote by parliament is entirely inadequate for effective training of a militia force for Canada.

I want to say a word or
two about No. 2 military district. I am surprised at the mover of the resolution, because he has been a distinguished soldier. May I say that the officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the units in Toronto are having the utmost difficulty to get men into their ranks. In view of the cuts made on military expenditures they find it difficult to pay the necessary costs. This vote is only about half what it used to be. Last Sunday the Toronto units held a parade in which some 6,060 men and officers took part. Frequently they have put their hands into their pockets, as have the friends of the units, to provide the necessary maintenance charges. Non-commissioned officers do the same thing for the men. If they receive a few dollars pay, on many occasions they put it into a common fund to maintain the unit. If we are to have such a limited amount, possibly it would be more in order to wipe out the militia altogether. Let us depend upon pacifism, purely and simply, if we are to reduce the vote, because we cannot have proper equipment under the present one. We have only about fifty per cent of the proper equipment in the non-permanent militia today, and the non-permanent militia are the back-bone of the permanent forces. While

everyone appreciates what the permanent force is doing, we know the non-permanent militia consists of young men in business and they are sick and tired of such small support from parliament. The government spends more money in support of that which our friends to the left depend upon, namely the League of Nations, and we get no results. This is an item from which we get practical results. I am surprised to see that the vote is so small, because I know it is becoming difficult to raise money to carry on the work.

I say this, too, that the expenditure is being used for the maintenance of an elaborate military establishment which is not getting practical results, and I am viewing the matter in a practical light. Further, we are reverting to that from which we suffered in 1914, at the outbreak of the war, when we were ordered to go into active service with obsolete training methods. It was often admitted by eminent military authorities that the headquarters staff at that time were not fully abreast of modern warfare. I think that is true of the training which is going on in the non-permanent militia units at this time. It is pathetic to watch the parade of some of our non-permanent militia units, and note the physical development of the young men in them, realizing at the same time the expenditures being made on the gewgaws of military training and on obsolete methods of training, when it is apparent that these same young men could be assisted in other and more practical ways. It is because I feel that this money is not being expended in a way

which secures practical value that I ask for a reduction by 11,000,000.

I feel it incumbent upon me to make some observations in view of the fact that my friend and colleague was in the Department of National Defence only a short time before the last election. The whole expenditure for national defence purposes was closely examined, on more than one occasion, by a committee of the cabinet, and it was the considered opinion of those who had the matter in hand that we could not adequately discharge our duty if we spent less than $10,000,000 a year. That opinion is not mine, nor yet that of any one man. It is the view arrived at after the closest analysis and scrutiny of every item. The real issue is: Shall we have any defence force in the country? Either we must not play with our defence force, to the extent of wasting money, or we must utilize it so that it will accomplish some purpose.
I would be the last man in the world to place my opinion against that of the hon. member for Vancouver North. He. knows whereof he speaks; he risked his life for his country on the field of battle. But I do say to him that the reports which we received are at variance with the views he has expressed. First, the military units are not at strength; that is obvious. I believe, however, that the numbers trained in those units have reached a high state of efficiency, according to modern standards of training. I do not believe it is fair to say that obsolete methods have been used. On the contrary it is my belief that the methods of training adopted in Canada are the modern which have developed in the light of the last conflict, and the knowledge gained therefrom.
For instance, mechanized artillery and mechanized branches of the service are known to everyone. Our medical service is as fine as can be found anywhere in the world. Our signalling corps has as fine a reputation and has received as ample training in electrical and other fields of knowledge allied to signalling as is found in any country, having in view the small number engaged in the work. When it comes down to a question of training of engineers, machine gun units or infantry units, I believe the standards which have been adopted are those used by the best instructors in the world. In addition to that there is annual inspection, and while for monetary reasons the camps cannot be maintained for long periods of time, they are maintained for periods of ten days or two

Supply-National Defence
weeks, and sometimes a little longer than that. The result has been that, according to my observation, the men have given an excellent account of themselves.
My friend from Vancouver North says that there are in this country various military divisions with district officers commanding. Can you have a district without a commandant? Can you get along without having someone in charge, and if you have a commandant, a D.O.C., you have every branch of the service represented, someone representing the engineers, someone representing the artillery, someone representing the medical services, the signalling corps, and so on. The engineering corps, for example, is a highly efficient corps. If you have any doubt about that, see what they did, for instance, at Calgary. There they undertook the work of constructing the barracks, laying it out and doing all that sort of work, doing it in a manner that has won the approval of the highest authorities; I do not know myself, of course. If we are going to have a service at all-and for my part I think we must, or say once and for all that we cease to be a community-if we are going to have it, as the minister has said, not for aggression, but purely as the nucleus of any defence it may be necessary for this country to resort to- and we all hope and pray to God that that may never be, but the facts stare us in the face-we must make these reasonable preparations for the defence of our country. I think the department does wonders in utilizing its money to the extent it does, in applying present day scientific methods to our military problems. I mention that because this is nothing new to me. I had the opinion which the hon. member for Vancouver North has expressed, and when we came into office I thought it would be possible to cut this item down substantially. I have no doubt that the minister has been through the very same experience. But what happens is that a committee of the cabinet closely investigates every item, and despite the attacks which may be made against those who are staff officers, they have a wide fund of knowledge and have given the benefit of it to successive governments, have recommended an improvement here and an improvement there, and the curtailment of expenditures when the minister has said that it was necessary to cut to the bone. We have done that, and I am told, not by these brass-hats to which reference is sometimes made, but by competent efficient men who have investigated these matters, that if we are going to maintain even a skeleton organization we cannot do it with
less money than this $10,000,000. That is the considered judgment of those who have had to deal with this pioblem. I say that because, as I have indicated, it has been experience which has taught me. I know, and every man who lives in a community knows exactly what the militia does. I have been privileged to be associated with some of these organizations as honorary colonel, and the honorary colonel-ship has been offered for an obvious reason, a very obvious one.
If you didn't have the money, you wouldn't be an honorary colonel.

When I think of what
I have seen with my own eyes, the amount of real sacrifice that has been made by men for no purpose in the world except their love of the work, not for swank, as someone has suggested, but because they are high-minded, public-spirited citizens who desire to do something for the welfare of their community, and have spent hours and days and weeks trying to train young men in the rudiments of self-control, self-reliance and self-respect, as Tennyson said, I am amazed at what has been done. Those three things, self-reliance, self-respect and self-control, constitute the basis of all the efforts we make in that regard, and after all that is a discipline very much to be desired. I have seen young men loose in their habits emerge, as a result of joining a militia unit and training for days and weeks and months, with those three qualities at least, selfrespect, self-reliance, self-control, very apparent. That is what I have seen, and I am sure that I but voice the sentiments of many people when I say that there are families who look back with satisfaction upon what has been done for some wayward sons by the operation of these militia units. The officers have been-and I was glad to hear the hon. member for Vancouver North admit it to be so-self-sacrificing, thinking only of the welfare of the community in which their services have been given. The real truth is that we have not nearly enough money in this country to give the service that we should give. It is pared down now to the very ibone, and I do not think it is possible, in the light of my own experience and observation to make the expenditure less and render service at all. When I compare our expenditure with that of other countries with our population in other parts of the world, I am amazed that we have accomplished as much as we have with the limited sums of money at our disposal. I think the committee would be well advised to
Supply-National Defence

negative this amendment, because it is one that, if carried, would destroy the active militia of this dominion at one fell swoop, and that would be the end of. it.
I have only one word more, and I apologize ter taking up time in connection with an item of this kind. The report to which the minister has alluded is one which was made after the most careful investigation of every phase of the matter, and it must be remembered that in practice our units are not full, and the number of men that are affected is much smaller than the number that there might be under a reorganized force at strength The same considerations which influenced the organization of the territorials under Lord Haldane have been the governing factors in determining the strength of our active militia, and notwithstanding anything which may be said to the contrary the truth is that but for the active militia in this country in 1914 Canada could not have done what she did. That, I think, is admitted by every man who knows the story of our effort in that great conflict.
